questions.question: What information does a MIDI Note On message contain?
options: Note number, velocity, and channel
Note number, sample rate, and channel
Frequency, amplitude, and duration
Note number, bit depth, and tempo
questions.explanation: A MIDI Note On message carries three pieces of data: the note number (0–127, identifying pitch), the velocity (0–127, indicating how hard the key was struck), and the channel (1–16, routing the message to the correct instrument). MIDI transmits performance data (not audio) so concepts like sample rate and bit depth do not apply.

questions.question: In General MIDI (GM), which channel is reserved for drum and percussion sounds?
options: Channel 1
Channel 10
Channel 16
Channel 8
questions.explanation: The General MIDI standard reserves channel 10 exclusively for drums and percussion. On this channel, each note number triggers a different drum sound (e.g., note 36 = bass drum, note 38 = snare) rather than a pitched instrument. This convention is shared across all GM-compatible devices.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes the key difference between MIDI and audio?
options: MIDI stores waveform data at a fixed sample rate; audio stores performance instructions
MIDI stores performance instructions (note, timing, velocity); audio stores the actual sound as a waveform
MIDI files are always larger than audio files because they contain more detail
MIDI can only be used with hardware synthesisers, not software
questions.explanation: MIDI is a performance protocol: it records what was played (note number, when, how hard) but contains no sound itself. Audio records the actual waveform of a sound. Because MIDI files only store instructions rather than waveform data, they are typically much smaller than audio files. The sound produced from MIDI depends entirely on the playback device or software instrument.

questions.question: A producer applies quantisation to a MIDI piano part. What does this process do?
options: Adjusts the pitch of each note to the nearest semitone
Compresses the dynamic range of the MIDI velocities
Moves note start times to align with the nearest rhythmic grid position
Converts MIDI data into an audio waveform
questions.explanation: Quantisation moves the timing of MIDI notes so they fall on (or closer to) a rhythmic grid: for example, the nearest 16th note. It corrects timing imprecision from live playing. Pitch correction is a separate process. Velocity editing affects dynamics. Rendering MIDI to audio is called 'bouncing' or 'freezing'.

questions.question: A MIDI Control Change (CC) message with controller number 64 is sent to a synthesiser. What does this control?
options: Modulation wheel depth
Master volume
Sustain pedal
Expression level
questions.explanation: CC64 is the standard General MIDI assignment for the sustain pedal. A value of 64–127 holds the sustain on; 0–63 releases it. Other standard assignments include CC1 (modulation wheel), CC7 (channel volume), and CC11 (expression). Knowing these standard controller numbers is expected at A-Level.

questions.question: Which MIDI message type is used to change the instrument sound (patch) on a given channel?
options: Control Change
Pitch Bend
Program Change
Note On
questions.explanation: A Program Change message instructs the receiving device to switch to a different instrument preset (patch). In General MIDI, Program Change 1 selects Acoustic Grand Piano, Program Change 57 selects Trumpet, and so on. Control Change messages adjust continuous parameters (e.g., volume, modulation), not the instrument selection.

questions.question: MIDI velocity uses 7-bit resolution. How many discrete velocity values are possible?
questions.explanation: 7-bit resolution means 2^7 = 128 possible values, numbered 0 to 127. Velocity 0 is treated as a Note Off event. Velocity 127 represents the maximum (hardest) strike. This 7-bit range applies to most MIDI data values including note numbers and many CC values.

questions.question: How many independent channels does the MIDI specification provide?
questions.explanation: MIDI supports 16 channels on a single cable or port. Each channel can carry a separate stream of note and control data, allowing up to 16 different instruments to be controlled simultaneously. Channel 10 is reserved for drums in General MIDI. For larger setups, multiple MIDI ports are used.

questions.question: The modulation wheel is assigned to which MIDI CC number in the General MIDI standard?
questions.explanation: CC1 is the General MIDI standard assignment for the modulation wheel. It is one of the most commonly used continuous controllers, typically mapped to vibrato depth or filter modulation on synthesisers. Remembering key CC assignments (CC1 (mod wheel), CC7 (volume), CC11 (expression), CC64 (sustain)) is important for A-Level.

questions.question: Explain what a MIDI Pitch Bend message does and why it is handled differently from other MIDI continuous controllers.
questions.sampleAnswer: A MIDI Pitch Bend message raises or lowers the pitch of notes on a channel in real time, typically mapped to a spring-loaded wheel that returns to centre. Unlike Control Change messages which use 7-bit resolution (128 steps), Pitch Bend uses 14-bit resolution (16,384 steps) to allow smooth, subtle pitch variation without audible stepping.
keyPoints: Pitch Bend changes the pitch of notes being played on that channel in real time
It uses 14-bit resolution (combining two 7-bit bytes) for smooth, continuous pitch movement
Higher resolution than standard CC messages prevents audible 'stepping' in the pitch glide
The centre value (no bend) is 8192 in 14-bit; the wheel returns to this position when released
questions.explanation: Pitch Bend is a dedicated MIDI message type separate from Control Change. Its 14-bit resolution (2^14 = 16,384 steps) is essential because pitch perception is highly sensitive. 7-bit resolution would produce audible stepped artefacts when bending smoothly between notes. This is why it has its own message status byte rather than sharing the CC format.

questions.question: Describe the purpose of MIDI Clock and explain how it is used to synchronise devices in a studio setup.
questions.sampleAnswer: MIDI Clock is a timing message transmitted 24 times per quarter note (24 ppqn) by a master device, such as a DAW or drum machine. Slave devices receive these clock pulses and use them to lock their internal tempo to the master. This allows sequencers, drum machines, and arpeggiators to stay in sync. MIDI Start, Stop, and Continue messages are used alongside MIDI Clock to control playback.
keyPoints: MIDI Clock sends 24 pulses per quarter note (24 ppqn)
One device acts as master (sends clock); others act as slaves (follow it)
Allows multiple hardware or software devices to share the same tempo
Accompanied by MIDI Start, Stop, and Continue transport messages
questions.explanation: MIDI Clock is a System Real-Time message, meaning it can be interleaved with other MIDI data in the data stream without interrupting it. The 24 ppqn rate provides enough resolution for tight synchronisation across a range of tempos. In modern studios, MIDI Clock may synchronise hardware synthesisers, drum machines, and effects units to a DAW's master tempo.

questions.question: A student records a live keyboard performance into their DAW. The timing is slightly inconsistent. They apply quantisation set to 1/16 note with 30% swing. Explain what each part of this setting does.
questions.sampleAnswer: The 1/16 note setting means each MIDI note is snapped to the nearest sixteenth-note grid position, correcting timing errors in the performance. The 30% swing setting offsets every other sixteenth note slightly later in time, creating a subtle rhythmic 'shuffle' feel rather than a rigid, mechanical grid. Higher swing percentages create a more pronounced shuffle or groove.
keyPoints: 1/16 note quantisation snaps note start times to the nearest sixteenth-note grid position
This corrects timing inaccuracies from the live performance
Swing offsets alternate grid positions (typically the 'off-beat' 16th notes) later in time
The result is a less rigid, more groove-based feel, higher swing = stronger shuffle
questions.explanation: Straight quantisation alone can make a performance sound mechanical by placing all notes on perfectly even grid positions. Swing (sometimes called 'groove') reintroduces rhythmic feel by pushing alternate notes back in time by a percentage of the grid interval. A 50% swing value produces an exact triplet feel; values between 50–75% produce varying degrees of shuffle. This is widely used in hip-hop, jazz, and funk production.

questions.question: What is the key difference between MIDI CC7 (Channel Volume) and CC11 (Expression)?
options: CC7 controls the overall channel level; CC11 is used for real-time dynamic variation within that level
CC7 controls panning; CC11 controls reverb depth
CC7 is 14-bit resolution; CC11 is 7-bit resolution
CC7 is only used in General MIDI; CC11 works in any MIDI specification
questions.explanation: CC7 sets the baseline volume level for a channel: think of it as the channel fader. CC11 (Expression) operates within that ceiling to add real-time dynamic shaping, such as swells and fades in an orchestral part. Using both together gives fine-grained control: CC7 sets the overall balance between instruments, and CC11 adds musical expression without disrupting the mix balance.

questions.question: A synthesiser responds to both channel aftertouch and polyphonic aftertouch. What is the key difference between these two message types?
options: Channel aftertouch applies the same pressure value to all notes on the channel; polyphonic aftertouch sends an independent pressure value per note
Polyphonic aftertouch only works on channel 10; channel aftertouch works on all channels
Channel aftertouch uses 14-bit resolution; polyphonic aftertouch uses 7-bit
Channel aftertouch is a System Exclusive message; polyphonic aftertouch is a Channel Voice message
questions.explanation: Channel aftertouch transmits a single pressure value that affects all held notes on that channel equally: if you press harder, every sounding note responds. Polyphonic (key) aftertouch sends individual pressure data for each note, so pressing harder on one key in a chord can add vibrato to that note alone. Polyphonic aftertouch generates significantly more MIDI data and is less commonly supported on standard keyboards.

questions.question: Which of the following is an advantage of MIDI transmitted over USB compared to traditional 5-pin DIN MIDI?
options: USB MIDI uses analogue signalling for lower latency
5-pin DIN supports more simultaneous channels than USB
USB can carry multiple MIDI ports over a single cable, along with power
5-pin DIN cables are bidirectional whereas USB is unidirectional
questions.explanation: A single USB connection can carry multiple virtual MIDI ports (each with 16 channels), eliminating the need for multiple DIN cables. USB also supplies bus power, so many controllers need no external power supply. Traditional 5-pin DIN is unidirectional (separate In/Out/Thru cables needed) and carries only one port (16 channels) per cable. However, DIN MIDI has the advantage of electrical isolation via its opto-isolated input, which prevents ground loops.

questions.question: What is the primary difference between a Standard MIDI File Type 0 and Type 1?
options: Type 0 supports General MIDI; Type 1 does not
Type 1 files are compressed; Type 0 files are uncompressed
Type 0 merges all channels into a single track; Type 1 stores each channel on a separate track
Type 0 files include audio data alongside MIDI; Type 1 files are MIDI-only
questions.explanation: A Type 0 SMF stores all MIDI data merged into one track, making it simple but harder to edit individual parts. A Type 1 SMF stores data on separate tracks (typically one per channel), preserving the multi-track arrangement from the DAW. Type 1 is preferred for editing and production work. Type 2 exists but is rarely used: it stores multiple independent patterns.

questions.question: Traditional MIDI uses a serial data rate of 31.25 kbaud. A 3-byte Note On message therefore takes approximately how many microseconds to transmit? (Each byte = 10 bits including start and stop bits.)
questions.explanation: At 31,250 bits per second, each bit takes 1/31250 = 32 μs. One byte (with start and stop bits) = 10 bits × 32 μs = 320 μs. A 3-byte message = 3 × 320 = 960 μs (just under 1 ms). This inherent transmission time is a source of MIDI latency, especially when many messages are sent in quick succession on a single DIN cable.

questions.question: MIDI Polyphonic Expression (MPE) uses one master channel and allocates the remaining channels as member channels. If the master channel is channel 1, how many member channels are available for individual note expression?
questions.explanation: MPE reserves one channel as the master (for global messages like sustain pedal) and assigns the remaining channels as member channels, one per active note. With channel 1 as master, channels 2–16 provide 15 member channels. This means up to 15 notes can each have independent pitch bend, slide, and pressure data simultaneously. Some MPE implementations use two zones (upper and lower), reducing the available members per zone.

questions.question: Explain what MIDI 2.0 improves over the original MIDI 1.0 specification, and why these improvements matter for modern music production.
questions.sampleAnswer: MIDI 2.0 increases resolution from 7-bit (128 values) to up to 32-bit for velocity and controller data, virtually eliminating audible stepping in parameter changes. It introduces bidirectional communication so devices can query each other's capabilities and auto-configure. It also adds per-note controllers (building on MPE concepts) and backwards compatibility with MIDI 1.0 devices.
keyPoints: Higher resolution: up to 32-bit for velocity and CC data (vs 7-bit in MIDI 1.0)
Bidirectional communication: devices negotiate capabilities automatically
Per-note controllers natively supported (pitch bend, pressure per note)
Backwards compatible with MIDI 1.0 devices and software
Eliminates audible stepping artefacts in fine controller movements
questions.explanation: MIDI 1.0 was designed in 1983 and its 7-bit resolution (128 steps) is a limitation for expressive performance: subtle fader moves or pitch bends can sound 'stepped'. MIDI 2.0 (ratified in 2020) addresses this with vastly higher resolution. Bidirectional communication means a controller can ask a synthesiser what parameters it supports and map them automatically, reducing manual setup. Per-note articulation is now a core feature rather than a workaround (as MPE was).

questions.question: A keyboard player notices that when they strike keys with varying force, the synthesiser responds differently depending on the selected velocity curve. Explain what a velocity curve is and describe how linear, logarithmic, and fixed curves differ in their musical effect.
questions.sampleAnswer: A velocity curve maps the physical force of a key strike to the MIDI velocity value sent. A linear curve provides a directly proportional response: medium force produces medium velocity. A logarithmic curve reaches higher velocity values more quickly with less force, making it easier to play loudly and suiting players with a lighter touch. A fixed curve ignores the physical force entirely and sends the same velocity value for every note, which is useful for parts that require uniform dynamics such as sequenced synthesiser lines.
keyPoints: Velocity curve maps physical key force to MIDI velocity value
Linear: proportional, medium force = medium velocity
Logarithmic: reaches higher values quickly with lighter touch
Fixed: constant velocity regardless of how hard the key is struck
Choice depends on playing style and musical context
questions.explanation: Velocity curves are set on the controller (keyboard), not the receiving instrument. They do not change the MIDI data format: they change the relationship between physical gesture and transmitted value. An exponential curve (opposite of logarithmic) requires harder playing to reach high velocities, suiting heavy-handed players. Understanding velocity curves helps students troubleshoot why the same keyboard can feel very different with different settings or when connected to different software instruments.
